How to read it: Hottest month of each year over land. Darker red means hotter.
How to read it: Pale green: short trees, about 5 m. Dark green: tall forest, over 45 m. Land only.
How to read it: Pale yellow: clear air. Orange to brown: thicker smoke, dust or haze.
How to read it: Purple and blue: cold, below 16 °C. Green and yellow: about 20 °C. Red: 28 °C and warmer.
How to read it: Scale from 405 to 430 parts per million. Yellow and orange: less CO₂. Dark red: more.
How to read it: The lines are currents at the sea surface. Their colour is the temperature of the water.

This is a time machine! It shows how hot the land gets each year, from 1950 to 2100. Darker red means hotter. Make the wave taller to add more pollution and see what scientists think could happen. As the land gets hotter, the notes climb higher and the music sounds more worried.
This is carbon dioxide, a gas that comes from cars, factories and fires. Too much of it makes Earth warmer.

This is the 'beauty shot version' of Perpetual Ocean 2: Western Boundary Currents. The visualization starts with a rotating globe showing ocean currents. The camera then zooms into the Kuroshio current, moves over the Indian Ocean to the Agulhas Current, then over to the Gulf Stream. The flows from the surface down to 600 meters deep are all white.
This map shows how warm the top of the sea is. Red means warm water. Blue and purple mean cold water. Warm seas give storms more energy.
This map shows the water hiding in the air. Blue is dry and red is very wet. Long wet streams are called atmospheric rivers, and they can bring lots of rain.
This record is a camera view, not a map, so it cannot be cut into zones. Zones work in the Time Machine, the sea surface currents and the lightning records.
This shows what floats in the air we breathe, like smoke and dust. Cleaner air is healthier for everyone.

This visualization depicts a global view of forest height data collected by the GEDI instrument aboard the International Space Station. Brown and dark green represent shorter vegetation. Bright green and white represent taller vegetation. This visualization uses data collected between April 2019 and April 2020. Height is exaggerated to depict variation at this scale.

This visualization shows sea surface current flows. The flows are colored by corresponding sea surface temperature data. This visualization is rendered for display on very high resolution devices like hyperwalls or for print media. This visualization was produced using model output from the joint MIT/JPL project entitled Estimating the Circulation and Climate of the Ocean, Phase II (ECCO2).
